findings.evidence: `pkg/executor/set.go:92` normalizes system var names via `name := strings.ToLower(v.Name)` but the SEMv2 read-only check uses unnormalized `v.Name` (`pkg/executor/set.go:141`). SEMv2 stores/looks up restricted variables by exact key (`pkg/util/sem/v2/sem.go:183-190`, `pkg/util/sem/v2/sem.go:270-276`). Parser preserves identifier casing for `SET [GLOBAL|SESSION] var=...` (`pkg/parser/parser.y:11154-11170`). Sysvar lookup is case-insensitive via lowercasing (`pkg/sessionctx/variable/variable.go:506-512`).
findings.fix: Use the normalized `name` (already lowercased) when checking SEMv2 read-only variables, e.g. call `semv2.IsReadOnlyVariable(name)` instead of `v.Name`. For defense-in-depth, also normalize SEMv2 config keys (store `restricted_variables[].name` as lower-case and lower-case on lookup) so enforcement is case-insensitive regardless of config casing.
findings.impact: SEMv2 read-only variable restrictions can be bypassed by using mixed-case variable names in `SET` statements (e.g., config restricts `sql_mode`, but `SET SQL_MODE=...` can skip the restriction). This undermines security/operational guarantees SEMv2 intends to enforce.
findings.later_fix_evidence: Not fixed up to `upstream/master` at `3b531d4e3d99cb988bebccb8f63a96afff0ec6cd`: `pkg/executor/set.go` still calls `semv2.IsReadOnlyVariable(v.Name)`.
findings.verify: With SEMv2 enabled, configure `restricted_variables` to include `{ "name": "sql_mode", "readonly": true }`. As a user without `RESTRICTED_VARIABLES_ADMIN`, run both `SET sql_mode='ANSI';` and `SET SQL_MODE='ANSI';`. After the fix, both variants should be rejected consistently (case-insensitive). Also verify `SET SESSION ...` and `SET GLOBAL ...` paths.
findings.what: SEMv2 read-only sysvar enforcement is case-sensitive and can be bypassed: `SetExecutor` lowercases the var name for sysvar resolution but checks `semv2.IsReadOnlyVariable` using the raw (case-preserving) name.

findings.evidence: `pkg/planner/core/planbuilder.go:6300-6302` does `checker := privilege.GetPrivilegeManager(b.ctx)` then immediately calls `checker.RequestDynamicVerification(...)` without a nil guard. `GetPrivilegeManager` can return nil (`pkg/privilege/privilege.go:136-141`). Some internal sessions explicitly bind a nil privilege manager (e.g., GC worker: `pkg/store/gcworker/gc_worker.go:241-245`).
findings.fix: Add a nil guard in `checkSEMStmt`, e.g. `if checker == nil || checker.RequestDynamicVerification(...) { ... }` (treat nil as trusted/internal), or at minimum return a clean permission error when `checker == nil` instead of dereferencing it.
findings.impact: If SEMv2 is enabled and a restricted SQL statement is planned in a context where the privilege manager is unset, TiDB can panic in the planner build path (risking connection drop or background worker failure, depending on caller recovery behavior).
findings.later_fix_evidence: Not fixed up to `upstream/master` at `3b531d4e3d99cb988bebccb8f63a96afff0ec6cd`: `checkSEMStmt` still dereferences `checker` without a nil check in `pkg/planner/core/planbuilder.go`.
findings.verify: Enable SEMv2 and configure `restricted_sql.sql` to include a common command (e.g. `SELECT`) for a controlled repro. Create an internal session with `privilege.BindPrivilegeManager(se, nil)` (as GC worker does) and execute a statement that matches the restricted rule; verify it does not panic (either allowed for internal sessions or returns a deterministic error).
findings.what: `PlanBuilder.checkSEMStmt` can dereference a nil privilege manager under SEMv2, leading to a panic when restricted SQL is encountered in sessions that intentionally disable privilege checking.
